notes.meaning: The Lord spoke to Moses shortly after Nadab and Abihu died for coming into God's presence the wrong way. God gave these new rules to protect the priests so they would not suffer the same fate. A safe and holy path was needed to keep fellowship alive between God and His people.

God warned that Aaron could not enter the Most Holy Place behind the curtain anytime he pleased, or he would die. The Lord made His presence known in a cloud over the mercy seat, the gold lid on the ark of the covenant. Approaching God's special presence requires deep reverence and careful obedience.

Aaron had to bring a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering before stepping into the sanctuary. A sin offering was an animal sacrifice that made things right with God by covering over human guilt. Aaron had to deal with his own sin before he could represent anyone else.

Aaron had to bathe in water and dress in plain white linen clothes instead of his usual colorful high priest robes. These simple garments showed personal humility and pure holiness before the Lord. Believers see in this a picture of Jesus setting aside heavenly splendor to serve in humility.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes Jewish traditions where the high priest began the day in his ornate golden garments and then changed into the plain white linen specifically for entering the Most Holy Place.

notes.meaning: The Israelite assembly supplied two male goats for a sin offering and one ram for a burnt offering. Even though two goats were given, they worked together as one combined sacrifice for the people. Both animals were needed to show two different sides of how God deals with sin.

Aaron brought the bull to make atonement for himself and his priestly household. Atonement means paying the penalty for wrong actions to bring sinners back into peace with God. Because Aaron was an imperfect human being, he needed cleansing before he could minister to others.

Aaron presented the two live goats before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle tent. Bringing them into public view showed that both animals were completely dedicated to God. Every part of this sacred day took place under the Lord's watchful eye.

Aaron cast lots over the two goats to determine which one belonged to the Lord and which would be the scapegoat. Casting lots left the final decision entirely in God's hands. One goat was appointed to be sacrificed, while the other was chosen to be sent away alive.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand the Hebrew title Azazel to be the name of a desert demon rather than a word describing the goat being sent away.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate translates Azazel as the emissary or scapegoat, though Catholic scholars also note the view that it refers to an evil desert spirit.

notes.meaning: Aaron took the goat selected for the Lord and prepared it as a sin offering. This animal died so its blood could pay the penalty for the people's disobedience. Its death points forward to Jesus shedding His blood to satisfy God's justice.

The second goat was kept alive before God to make atonement and was then sent into the open wilderness. While the first goat showed the penalty of sin being paid by death, the live goat showed sins being removed far away. Together, they picture full forgiveness and the complete removal of guilt.

Aaron slaughtered the bull as a sin offering to atone for himself and his fellow priests. He had to confess his sins and offer a substitutionary sacrifice before doing anything else. Only when his own record was clean could he safely enter God's presence.

Aaron filled a pan with hot coals from the altar and carried two handfuls of sweet ground incense inside the curtain. Taking fire and incense into the inner room prepared the way for the blood offering. The rising fragrant smoke represented holy prayers ascending to God.

Aaron placed the incense on the hot coals so that a cloud of fragrant smoke covered the mercy seat above the ark. This smoke shielded Aaron from looking directly upon God's bright glory, protecting him from death. It demonstrated that sinners can only approach God through intercession and mediation.

Aaron took the bull's blood and sprinkled it once onto the front of the mercy seat and seven times on the ground before it. In Scripture, the number seven points to perfection and completeness. The sprinkled blood testified that a life had been given to satisfy divine justice.

Aaron went outside, killed the people's goat, and carried its blood into the Most Holy Place. He sprinkled its blood on and in front of the mercy seat just as he had done with the bull's blood. This brought the sign of the nation's cleansing right before God's heavenly throne.

Aaron made atonement for the sanctuary because the rebellions and sins of the Israelites had made it unclean. Even though the tabernacle was holy, standing in the middle of a sinful nation brought spiritual pollution onto it. Cleansing the sacred space allowed God to continue living with His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often describe this ceremony as an annual ritual purge designed to scrub away the accumulated pollution that human rebellion brought upon the sacred sanctuary space.

notes.meaning: No other person was allowed inside the tabernacle while Aaron made atonement in the Most Holy Place. Aaron had to complete the entire reconciliation by himself from start to finish. This points to Jesus Christ as the only Mediator who could accomplish the work of salvation alone.

Aaron went out to the altar of the Lord and applied the mixed blood of the bull and the goat to its four horns. The horns stood at each corner and symbolized strength, so touching them with blood cleansed the place of daily sacrifice. This showed that both priests and regular people shared the same need for forgiveness.

Aaron sprinkled blood on the altar seven times with his finger to purify and dedicate it. This sevenfold sprinkling wiped out the spiritual uncleanness brought by the people's sins over the past year. It restored the altar as a clean, holy place for future worship.

Once the cleansing of the Most Holy Place, the tent, and the altar was complete, Aaron brought forward the live goat. Every part of the sanctuary had now been reconciled and purified by blood. The ceremony was now ready to deal with the guilt of the people themselves.

Aaron placed both hands on the live goat's head and confessed all the sins and rebellions of Israel over it. Laying on hands showed that the nation's guilt was transferred onto the animal as their substitute. An appointed man then took charge of leading the goat away into the wilderness.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Seventh-day Adventist teaching views the scapegoat as a figure of Satan, who will eventually bear the final blame and punishment for the sins of the redeemed.

notes.meaning: The live goat carried all the people's sins into an empty, lonely land where the man released it. This showed the people that God had sent their guilt far away, never to return. Believers see in this how Christ carries our sins away so they are remembered no more.

Aaron returned to the tent, took off the white linen clothes he had worn in the inner sanctuary, and left them there. Those garments were set apart solely for the sacred work of atonement. Putting them aside signaled that the work inside the Most Holy Place was completely finished.

Aaron washed his body in a holy place and dressed in his regular high priest robes. He then went out to offer burnt offerings for himself and the people to show renewed surrender to God. Forgiven sinners respond by dedicating their whole lives back to the Lord.

Aaron burned the rich fat from the sin offerings on the altar of burnt offering. Under the law, the fat portions were considered the richest part of the animal and belonged solely to the Lord. Burning them was a pleasing aroma that honored God's goodness.

The man who led the scapegoat into the wilderness had to wash his clothes and bathe before re-entering the camp. Because the goat carried the defilement of the people's sins, anyone who touched it became ceremonially unclean. This showed how deeply sin defiles everything it touches.

The bodies of the bull and goat whose blood entered the inner sanctuary were taken outside the camp and burned completely. None of their meat could be eaten because they had borne the curse of sin. The New Testament points to this to show that Jesus died outside the city gate to make us holy.

The person who burned the animal carcasses outside the camp had to wash his clothes and bathe in water before returning. Even handling the remains of a sin offering caused ceremonial uncleanness. This rule reminded the people that dealing with sin always leaves a mark that requires washing.

God made this day an enduring rule, to be kept on the tenth day of the seventh month by fasting and resting from work. Both native Israelites and foreigners living among them had to observe it. Laying aside regular food and labor gave everyone time to reflect on their need for mercy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary highlights this observance as an absolute annual fast from all food and labor from sunset on the ninth day until sunset on the tenth day.

notes.meaning: God promised that on this day atonement would be completed so the people would stand clean from all their sins. The Lord provided the way to wipe out their guilt and restore peace. This gave the Israelites deep comfort that their relationship with God was secure.

This day was a Sabbath of complete rest, where the people humbled their souls before the Lord forever. Setting aside regular work allowed them to focus entirely on repentance and God's holiness. Spiritual rest comes when guilt is removed and peace with God is found.

Future high priests anointed to succeed their fathers were required to carry out this exact service in the holy linen garments. The high priestly office would pass down through generations without change. Every high priest had to approach God in the same attitude of humble obedience.

The high priest made atonement for the Most Holy Place, the tabernacle tent, the altar, the priests, and all the people. Every single part of the worship space and every member of the nation was covered by this one cleansing. God's mercy reached from the leaders down to the humblest citizen.

This annual day of atonement remained an ongoing rule for Israel, and Aaron obeyed everything the Lord commanded. Repeating the sacrifices every year showed that animal blood could never take away sin permanently. Believers see that this yearly pattern pointed forward to Jesus Christ, who offered one final sacrifice forever.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic theology sees these yearly Old Testament sacrifices as figures pointing toward Christ's sacrifice on the Cross, which is continually renewed in an unbloody way in the holy Mass.
